title: Could vaccines cure cancer?
transcript:
Hi Phil.
Hi Georgie.
Phil, have you had many vaccines in your life? So, these are injections to protect you from diseases.
Oh, I've had loads. I had all the ones you have when you’re a child, but I've also had some for travelling and working abroad so… yeah, I've had lots.
OK. Well, many of us will have had vaccines to stop us getting common diseases such as flu or Covid 19, but could injections help us fight more complicated diseases too? In this episode of 6 Minute English, we'll be looking at some new research that has scientists very excited, and we'll be asking the question, 'Could vaccines cure cancer?'
OK. Let's start with a quiz question, Phil. There are lots of different types of cancer affecting many parts of the body, but according to the World Health Organisation, what is the most common cancer worldwide? Is it: a) lung cancer, b) skin cancer, or c) stomach cancer?
Well, I don't know. I'm going to guess b) skin cancer.
Well, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.
Right. Now, this idea of a vaccine that could cure cancer sounds really interesting. Could you tell us a bit more about it, Georgie?
Well, scientists have been trying to develop a cancer vaccine for quite a long time. If you think about many existing cancer treatments, such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy, these have quite a few side effects. But the idea is that a cancer vaccine would help the body's natural immune system help fight the disease, which could have fewer side effects and also be more effective. Scientists are particularly hopeful about a new vaccine developed to treat skin cancer. BBC Radio 4 programme Inside Science has been hearing about the latest research. Cancer cell biologist Anne Willis spoke to presenter Tom Whipple.
I guess this moment has been quite a long time coming, hasn't it? There's been some false dawns in cancer vaccines.
I mean, there's been a lot of work in this space, and it's all been very encouraging, particularly in the animal models, but getting this to translate into humans can be a much harder, longer process, so it's very exciting that there's this breakthrough – apparent breakthrough – that's come through today.
Tom says that the development of the cancer vaccine has been a long time coming, and this means that it's taken a lot of time to achieve.
Yes. Tom also says there have been some false dawns, an expression meaning that something looks like it's improving when it's actually not.
Anne says there's been a lot of work in this space. Space here means field of research – so, in this context, research into cancer vaccines.
Scientists think they might have made a breakthrough. That means they've made significant progress.
And Georgie, these vaccines that we're talking about, they aren't quite like the ones that we're all familiar with, are they? This isn't a vaccine to prevent you from getting skin cancer, is it?
No. The vaccine being tested is used to treat people after they've had a tumour removed. It's used to target any cancer cells that have been spread around the body, to stop the cancer from coming back, and the vaccine is made specially for each patient by looking at the cancerous cells in the tumour that's been removed. Anne Willis explained more to BBC Radio 4's Inside Science.
So, cancer cells are very different from normal cells. They contain lots of mutations. So, you sequence the DNA of the cancer cell to work out how it's different from a normal cell. And then, particularly for the bits of the cancer that's different on the surface of the cell, you take those bits of DNA and then you put them into the RNA vaccine, and then they'll make these bits of proteins that get recognised by the immune system. So, it's a way of priming the immune system to the cancer.
Anne is saying that the scientists work out what in the cancer cells is different and put these bits into the vaccine.
Right. The vaccine then becomes a way of priming the immune system to cancer. If you prime something, you get it ready. The vaccine basically helps the immune system get better at recognising and fighting cancer cells in the body.
Now, that sounds like some really clever science here. Could it make a big difference, Georgie?
Well, more trials are needed, but scientists are hopeful. Here's Anne Willis again talking to Tom Whipple, presenter of Inside Science.
Are you excited?
Oh, I mean, very! I'm just, you know… anything that will improve lives of cancer patients is always wonderful. And actually, seeing that this extraordinary technology is, sort of, starting to reach its promise – this is very exciting for everybody.
So, Anne is excited. She says that after a long time working on this technology, it's starting to reach its promise. And promise here means positive potential.
OK. Phil, I think it's time I revealed the answer to my question. I asked you, "What is the most common form of cancer worldwide?" You said skin cancer, but the answer is actually lung cancer. In 2024, there were an estimated 2.4 million cases worldwide, according to the World Health Organisation.
OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with the expression a long time coming, which means something has taken a long time to achieve.
A false dawn is when something appears to be improving, when it actually isn't.
Space can mean field of research.
A breakthrough refers to making significant progress with something.
If you prime something, you get it ready.
And promise can mean positive potential.
Once again, our six minutes are up. Test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website. And that's bbclearningenglish.com.
Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
Bye.

sentences.text: Hi Phil.
sentences.translation: 你好，菲尔。

sentences.text: Hi Georgie.
sentences.translation: 你好，乔治。

sentences.text: Phil, have you had many vaccines in your life?
sentences.translation: 菲尔，你一生中打过很多疫苗吗？

sentences.text: So, these are injections to protect you from diseases.
sentences.translation: 就是那些保护你不生病的注射针剂。

sentences.text: Oh, I've had loads.
sentences.translation: 哦，我打过不少。

sentences.text: I had all the ones you have when you’re a child, but I've also had some for travelling and working abroad so… yeah, I've had lots.
sentences.translation: 小时候该打的我都打了，后来出国旅行和工作也打了些……所以，是的，打过很多。

sentences.text: OK.
sentences.translation: 好的。

sentences.text: Well, many of us will have had vaccines to stop us getting common diseases such as flu or Covid 19, but could injections help us fight more complicated diseases too?
sentences.translation: 我们很多人都打过预防流感或新冠这类常见病的疫苗，但注射疫苗也能帮我们对抗更复杂的疾病吗？

sentences.text:
In this episode of 6 Minute English, we'll be looking at some new research that has scientists very excited, and we'll be asking the question, 'Could vaccines cure cancer?'
OK.
sentences.translation: 在本期《六分钟英语》中，我们会看到一些让科学家非常兴奋的新研究，并探讨一个问题：疫苗能治愈癌症吗？

sentences.text: Let's start with a quiz question, Phil.
sentences.translation: 好的。

sentences.text: There are lots of different types of cancer affecting many parts of the body, but according to the World Health Organisation, what is the most common cancer worldwide?
sentences.translation: 先来个测验题吧，菲尔。

sentences.text: Is it: a) lung cancer, b) skin cancer, or c) stomach cancer?
sentences.translation: 癌症有很多种，会影响身体很多部位，但根据世界卫生组织的数据，全世界最常见的癌症是什么？

sentences.text: Well, I don't know.
sentences.translation: 是：a) 肺癌，b) 皮肤癌，还是 c) 胃癌？

sentences.text: I'm going to guess b) skin cancer.
sentences.translation: 嗯，我不知道。

sentences.text: Well, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.
sentences.translation: 我猜 b) 皮肤癌。

sentences.text: Right.
sentences.translation: 节目最后我们再揭晓答案。

sentences.text: Now, this idea of a vaccine that could cure cancer sounds really interesting.
sentences.translation: 好。

sentences.text: Could you tell us a bit more about it, Georgie?
sentences.translation: 这个能治愈癌症的疫苗想法听起来真有意思。

sentences.text: Well, scientists have been trying to develop a cancer vaccine for quite a long time.
sentences.translation: 能给我们多讲讲吗，乔治？

sentences.text: If you think about many existing cancer treatments, such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy, these have quite a few side effects.
sentences.translation: 科学家尝试研发癌症疫苗已经很久了。

sentences.text: But the idea is that a cancer vaccine would help the body's natural immune system help fight the disease, which could have fewer side effects and also be more effective.
sentences.translation: 现有的很多癌症治疗方法，比如放疗和化疗，都有不少副作用。

sentences.text: Scientists are particularly hopeful about a new vaccine developed to treat skin cancer.
sentences.translation: 而这个想法是，癌症疫苗能帮助身体的天然免疫系统来对抗疾病，副作用可能更少，也更有效。

sentences.text: BBC Radio 4 programme Inside Science has been hearing about the latest research.
sentences.translation: 科学家对一种新研发的治疗皮肤癌的疫苗特别有信心。

sentences.text: Cancer cell biologist Anne Willis spoke to presenter Tom Whipple.
sentences.translation: BBC Radio 4 的《Inside Science》节目介绍了这项最新研究。

sentences.text: I guess this moment has been quite a long time coming, hasn't it?
sentences.translation: 癌症细胞生物学家安妮·威利斯接受了主持人汤姆·惠普尔的采访。

sentences.text: There's been some false dawns in cancer vaccines.
sentences.translation: 我觉得这一刻真是来得不容易，对吧？

sentences.text: I mean, there's been a lot of work in this space, and it's all been very encouraging, particularly in the animal models, but getting this to translate into humans can be a much harder, longer process, so it's very exciting that there's this breakthrough – apparent breakthrough – that's come through today.
sentences.translation: 癌症疫苗领域曾出现过一些虚假的希望。

sentences.text: Tom says that the development of the cancer vaccine has been a long time coming, and this means that it's taken a lot of time to achieve.
sentences.translation: 这个领域做了很多工作，一直很令人鼓舞，尤其是在动物实验中，但要转化到人身上可能要难得多、久得多，所以今天能有这个突破——表面上的突破——真是非常令人兴奋。

sentences.text: Yes.
sentences.translation: 汤姆说癌症疫苗的研发是个漫长的过程，意思是花了很长时间才实现。

sentences.text: Tom also says there have been some false dawns, an expression meaning that something looks like it's improving when it's actually not.
sentences.translation: 是的。

sentences.text: Anne says there's been a lot of work in this space.
sentences.translation: 汤姆还说曾出现过一些“虚假的黎明”，这个短语指某事看似在好转，实际并非如此。

sentences.text: Space here means field of research – so, in this context, research into cancer vaccines.
sentences.translation: 安妮说在这个领域做了很多工作。

sentences.text: Scientists think they might have made a breakthrough.
sentences.translation: 这里的“领域”指的是研究领域，也就是癌症疫苗的研究。

sentences.text: That means they've made significant progress.
sentences.translation: 科学家认为他们可能取得了突破。

sentences.text: And Georgie, these vaccines that we're talking about, they aren't quite like the ones that we're all familiar with, are they?
sentences.translation: 意思是他们取得了重大进展。

sentences.text: This isn't a vaccine to prevent you from getting skin cancer, is it?
sentences.translation: 乔治，我们说的这种疫苗，其实和大家熟悉的疫苗不太一样，对吧？

sentences.text: No.
sentences.translation: 它不是预防你得皮肤癌的疫苗，对吧？

sentences.text: The vaccine being tested is used to treat people after they've had a tumour removed.
sentences.translation: 对。

sentences.text: It's used to target any cancer cells that have been spread around the body, to stop the cancer from coming back, and the vaccine is made specially for each patient by looking at the cancerous cells in the tumour that's been removed.
sentences.translation: 正在测试的疫苗是给切除了肿瘤的人使用的。

sentences.text: Anne Willis explained more to BBC Radio 4's Inside Science.
sentences.translation: 它用来对付已经扩散到全身的癌细胞，防止癌症复发，而且这种疫苗是通过分析切除肿瘤中的癌细胞，为每位患者量身定制的。

sentences.text: So, cancer cells are very different from normal cells.
sentences.translation: 安妮·威利斯向 BBC Radio 4 的《Inside Science》做了更多解释。

sentences.text: They contain lots of mutations.
sentences.translation: 癌细胞和正常细胞非常不同。

sentences.text: So, you sequence the DNA of the cancer cell to work out how it's different from a normal cell.
sentences.translation: 它们含有很多突变。

sentences.text: And then, particularly for the bits of the cancer that's different on the surface of the cell, you take those bits of DNA and then you put them into the RNA vaccine, and then they'll make these bits of proteins that get recognised by the immune system.
sentences.translation: 所以你要对癌细胞的 DNA 进行测序，搞清楚它和正常细胞有什么不同。

sentences.text: So, it's a way of priming the immune system to the cancer.
sentences.translation: 然后，尤其是癌细胞表面那些不同的部分，你把这些 DNA 片段放进 RNA 疫苗里，它们就会制造出这些蛋白片段，被免疫系统识别。

sentences.text: Anne is saying that the scientists work out what in the cancer cells is different and put these bits into the vaccine.
sentences.translation: 这就是一种让免疫系统提前对癌症做好准备的方法。

sentences.text: Right.
sentences.translation: 安妮是说，科学家找出癌细胞里不同的地方，把这些片段放进疫苗。

sentences.text: The vaccine then becomes a way of priming the immune system to cancer.
sentences.translation: 对。

sentences.text: If you prime something, you get it ready.
sentences.translation: 这样疫苗就成了让免疫系统提前“备战”癌症的一种方式。

sentences.text: The vaccine basically helps the immune system get better at recognising and fighting cancer cells in the body.
sentences.translation: “priming”就是把某样东西准备好。

sentences.text: Now, that sounds like some really clever science here.
sentences.translation: 这个疫苗基本上是帮助免疫系统更善于识别和对抗体内的癌细胞。

sentences.text: Could it make a big difference, Georgie?
sentences.translation: 听起来这真是很聪明的科学。

sentences.text: Well, more trials are needed, but scientists are hopeful.
sentences.translation: 它能带来很大改变吗，乔治？

sentences.text: Here's Anne Willis again talking to Tom Whipple, presenter of Inside Science.
sentences.translation: 还需要更多试验，但科学家们抱有希望。

sentences.text: Are you excited?
sentences.translation: 再来听听安妮·威利斯对《Inside Science》主持人汤姆·惠普尔说的话。

sentences.text: Oh, I mean, very!
sentences.translation: 你兴奋吗？

sentences.text: I'm just, you know… anything that will improve lives of cancer patients is always wonderful.
sentences.translation: 哦，当然，非常兴奋！

sentences.text: And actually, seeing that this extraordinary technology is, sort of, starting to reach its promise – this is very exciting for everybody.
sentences.translation: 你知道，任何能改善癌症患者生活的东西都是极好的。

sentences.text: So, Anne is excited.
sentences.translation: 看到这项了不起的技术开始兑现它的潜力，这对所有人来说都非常令人兴奋。

sentences.text: She says that after a long time working on this technology, it's starting to reach its promise.
sentences.translation: 所以安妮很兴奋。

sentences.text: And promise here means positive potential.
sentences.translation: 她说研究这项技术很长时间之后，它开始兑现自己的潜力了。

sentences.text: OK.
sentences.translation: 这里的“潜力”指的是积极的可能。

sentences.text: Phil, I think it's time I revealed the answer to my question.
sentences.translation: 好。

sentences.text: I asked you, "What is the most common form of cancer worldwide?" You said skin cancer, but the answer is actually lung cancer.
sentences.translation: 菲尔，该揭晓测验答案了。

sentences.text: In 2024, there were an estimated 2.4 million cases worldwide, according to the World Health Organisation.
sentences.translation: 我问你“全世界最常见的癌症是什么？”你答的是皮肤癌，但其实答案是肺癌。

sentences.text: OK.
sentences.translation: 根据世界卫生组织的数据，2024 年全球估计有 240 万个病例。

sentences.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with the expression a long time coming, which means something has taken a long time to achieve.
sentences.translation: 好的。

sentences.text: A false dawn is when something appears to be improving, when it actually isn't.
sentences.translation: 我们来回顾一下本节目学到的词汇，先从“a long time coming”开始，指某事花了很长时间才实现。

sentences.text: Space can mean field of research.
sentences.translation: “虚假的黎明”指某事看似在好转，实际上并没有。

sentences.text: A breakthrough refers to making significant progress with something.
sentences.translation: “Space”可以指研究领域。

sentences.text: If you prime something, you get it ready.
sentences.translation: “突破”指在某事上取得重大进展。

sentences.text: And promise can mean positive potential.
sentences.translation: “Priming”就是把某样东西准备好。

sentences.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.
sentences.translation: 而“潜力”可以指积极的可能。

sentences.text: Test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.
sentences.translation: 又到了节目结束的时候。

sentences.text: And that's bbclearningenglish.com.
sentences.translation: 去我们网站的练习册测试一下你学到了什么。

sentences.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
sentences.translation: 网址是 bbclearningenglish.com。

sentences.text: Bye.
sentences.translation: 感谢收听，再见。
